newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia assembly to start cabinet hearings Friday.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia assembly to start cabinet hearings Friday.

text.p: The Slovenian parliament said on Thursday it would begin hearing ministerial candidates on Friday and would probably vote on Prime Minister-designate Janez Drnovsek's line-up at the end of next week.

Hearings will continue until February 25 and a vote is likely on February 27 or 28. The make-or-break vote for Drnovsek comes almost four months after a general election that left no single party with a clear mandate.
Drnovsek, prime minister since 1992 and leader of the centre-left Liberal Democrats, is trying to form a government in coalition with the conservative People's Party and pensioners' party Desus.
Two weeks ago parliament scuppered Drnovsek's attempt to build a leftist cabinet with the ex-communists, the United List of Social Democrats.

Analysts say he has a better chance of succeeding this time around. If he fails to win parliamentary approval for at least two-thirds of his team, President Milan Kucan will have to nominate a new prime minister.
"It would be quite a surprise if the new line-up is not approved by the parliament," an analyst said.

Together the coalition parties hold 49 out of 90 seats in parliament. They are also expected to gain the support of two representatives of Hungarian and Italian minorities and an independent delegate.
If elected, the new cabinet is unlikely to bring major changes to Slovenian foreign, economic and social policy.
"The main ministerial posts are held by the same team as in the last government so I do not expect any major changes," said Igor Luksic, professor of politics at Ljubljana University.
The Liberal Democrats look certain to provide the next foreign and finance ministers, while the People's Party will get the defence and agricultural portfolios.
Zoran Thaler, foreign minister prior to May 1996, is again a candidate for the post this time around. Mitja Gaspari, finance minister for the past four years, will probably keep his post.
Among the main goals of the new government will be full membership of NATO by the year 1999 and entry into the European Union as soon as possible. At home it will aim to undertake pension reform.
The new government will be the third since Slovenia's independence from the former Yogoslavia in 1991.
